doc:
/**
 * Week 2 — the endings that decide most of the spellings a learner meets next.
 *
 * -tion and -sion, -able and -ible, the silent letters English keeps from
 * languages it borrowed from, the three sounds of -ed, and the -ough family
 * that spells six different vowels with four letters.
 *
 * The misspellings stay diagnostic rather than random. `nashion` and `acsion`
 * are what a learner writes when they spell -tion the way it sounds;
 * `possable` and `terrable` are the -ible half of a rule with no audible
 * difference; `wierd`, `nieghbour` and `hieght` are the i-before-e rule applied
 * where it does not hold. Several pairs are in deliberately together —
 * `advice`/`advise`, `effect`/`affect`, `except`/`accept`, `whether`/`weather`,
 * `break`/`brake`, `whole`/`hole` — because each is the other's commonest
 * misspelling and teaching them apart is the point.
 */

days.title: Nation, station, question
days.focus: The -tion and -sion endings, and why they sound the same and are spelled apart.

days.title: Able and ible
days.focus: A rule with no audible difference: comfortable but possible, and how to tell.

days.title: Letters you do not say
days.focus: Silent k, w, b, gh and h — knee, wrist, thumb, honest, island.

days.title: The three sounds of -ed
days.focus: Walked, opened and wanted end in /t/, /d/ and /ɪd/, and the spelling never changes.

days.title: Words that trade places
days.focus: Advice and advise, effect and affect, except and accept, whether and weather.

days.title: Tough, though, through
days.focus: The -ough family, and the numbers and seasons that carry silent letters too.

days.title: Endings that build words
days.focus: -ness, -ly and -age: happiness, carefully, message — and the doubling they do not cause.
